https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.title: Police hit back at critics after M25 climate protests
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.text:
Activists exploit legal loopholes to frustrate the police and public, the head of the Police Federation said in defence of the handling of the M25 protests.
Drivers were stuck for hours at five junctions blocked off by 100 environmental protesters from Insulate Britain as officers tried to clear them, causing tailbacks several miles long. At least 77 people were arrested.
One furious driver was filmed trying to drag a demonstrator out of the road before police intervened.
John Apter told The Times that the protest on Monday was an “exceptional situation” that took time to clear. “If we are robust we get criticised. If we take a more measured approach we get criticised,” he said. “The protesters are not daft people, they do what they do to cause maximum effect and organisers know the law.
“Officers who turn up and are faced with that don’t have the resources to start scooping people up and throwing them in the back of vans — they don’t. Sometimes these things take time.”
He added: “I understand the criticism from the public who were stuck in traffic. What sticks in the throat is armchair critics and retired officers giving uninformed views on social media without knowing the facts.
“Police officers don’t turn up to jobs with an intention to prolong the frustration and anger of the public. They will always do their best but sadly in situations like these their best is usually not considered good enough.”
A group on Twitter called UK Police Pensioners United accused officers of “aiding and abetting” the M25 protest by “slow reactions and decisions”. It said: “None of the M25 forces covered themselves in glory.”
A motorist caught up in the chaos on the London orbital said he had been stuck for more than three hours with his two children, aged two and six months.
He wrote on social media: “I am seething at how irresponsible and selfish their demonstration is. It is ill-considered and poorly executed.
“I am all for change and reducing fuel poverty but there are more sensible ways to lobby and protest.”
Another road user threatened to take matters into their own hands if the police did not clear the protesters, saying: “These climate change imbeciles have no legal basis upon which to block the highway especially as such nonsense could potentially hold up emergency services and cost lives.”
Hertfordshire police insisted they had responded swiftly to the protests with the first arrests taking place at 9.20am, just over an hour after the demonstration began, with the road reopening an hour later.
Chief Inspector Paul Austin, of Essex police, said: “This incident caused significant disruption and our officers worked to resolve it as quickly and safely as possible.”
Policing protests has become a more complex issue for forces after a Supreme Court ruling that obstruction can be a legitimate and lawful form of protest.
The Ziegler judgment, handed down in June, ruled that the exercising of protest rights could constitute a “lawful excuse” for obstructing the highway, even if the protest is considered disruptive.
The ruling has been used to overturn a number of convictions related to Extinction Rebellion protests.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.title: M25 protests: activists block traffic for second day this week
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.text:
Protesters calling for the government to fund home insulation have brought parts of the M25 to a standstill for the second day in a week.
In a near replica of a demonstration on Monday, 89 activists for Insulate Britain set up roadblocks at six locations on the M25 in Surrey, Kent and Hertfordshire, causing miles of tailbacks.
Some have glued themselves to the tarmac in an effort to stymie attempts by police to forcibly remove them from the road, a spokeswoman for Insulate Britain said. As of 2pm, 71 people had been arrested.
The group, which has links to Extinction Rebellion (XR), said that it planned further motorway protests later in the week and would continue to occupy the roads until its demands are met.
A group of 15 activists at junction 8 near Reigate in Surrey were able to get onto the motorway by phoning the police who closed the road for them. At 8am the group climbed down onto the hard shoulder and rang 101, the non-emergency police line, and told call handlers where they were. Surrey Police were then required to stop the traffic themselves in order to prevent an accident happening, allowing the protesters to sit in the road.
By 8.50am all of the demonstrators had been arrested and carried into police vans, enabling the road to reopen.
Previously, the group had only set up blocks at traffic lights and roundabouts. They did a trial-run of the new tactic on Monday.
A crash near junction 9 involving four vehicles led to a woman in her 50s being airlifted to hospital with serious injuries.
Surrey Police said the investigation into the collision was ongoing, adding: “It is too early in the investigation to know if these two incidents were linked.”
Kwasi Kwarteng, the business secretary, said the protests were putting lives at risk. He tweeted: “These actions are not only highly disruptive to those going to work and transporting vital goods, but are putting lives at risk on a busy motorway.
“Not to mention the resulting traffic delays will only add to vehicle emissions.”
A Home Office source said that police should be able to immediately arrest protesters who disrupt motorways: “There will be members of the public across the UK who will be looking at this and asking why the police didn’t act sooner. It strengthens the argument for exactly why we need the new powers contained in our Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Bill.”
The source pointed to new powers in the legislation that will give the police the power to impose stricter conditions on static protests, such as time limits equivalent to rallies. The bill will also allow for tighter restrictions on protests that cause disruption to the public.
The locations targeted by today’s protest were junction 23 at South Mimms; the main carriageway of the M25 anti-clockwise in Surrey between junction 9 and junction 8; junction 1b near the Dartford crossing; junction 25 on the M25; the A10 in Hertfordshire; and junction 10 of the A3 in Surrey.
Among those arrested was Diana Warner, 62, a retired GP from Bristol, who has previously been arrested for actions with XR.
“People are living in damp, unfit conditions and are having to choose between paying either for fuel or food,” she said. “This is a crisis of equity between rich and poor.”
Superintendent Adam Willmot, of Hertfordshire police, said: “Policing protests can be challenging and complex, and as such we have a dedicated command team managing the situation.
“We also have specialist resources working to resolve the situation as quickly as possible, with minimum disruption to the public and local businesses. Officers are highly trained, and operations follow clear, national standards.
“Our officers were on the scene within minutes of us being alerted to the protest, and attempted to engage with the group, working to balance the rights of people to protest with the rights of those affected by their presence.
“However, protesters ignored repeated requests from officers to move to a safer and less disruptive location, and alleged that they had glued themselves to the road, making it clear that their aim was to cause as much disruption as possible.”
Among those behind Insulate Britain, which was formed over the summer, is Roger Hallam, co-founder of XR, who sits on the groups’ strategic committee.
He was expelled from XR last year after comments about the Holocaust that appeared to play down the significance of the genocide.
Hallam owns a farmhouse in Wales, which was described as “poorly insulated” in an official energy performance certificate, the Daily Mail reported.
Police chiefs have admitted the difficulties in dealing with protesters who occupy motorways.
John Apter, head of the Police Federation, told The Times yesterday: “If we are robust we get criticised. If we take a more measured approach we get criticised.
“The protesters are not daft people, they do what they do to cause maximum effect and organisers know the law.”
On Monday drivers and protesters when activists set up roadblocks at five locations, causing tailbacks several miles long.
Video showed angry drivers trying to hoist the protesters out of the road, before police arrived and formed a cordon between the two groups. The activists were later arrested and taken away in vans.
Police forces from across the southeast were called to deal with the disruption, and at least 74 arrests were made. Edmund King, president of the AA, described the action as “incredibly dangerous” and said that it had put lives at risk.
Insulate Britain’s tactics reflect those of XR, who have used civil disobedience to shut down parts of London by having protesters sit on main thoroughfares.
A spokeswoman for the group said that the decision to blockade major roads had been an “unpleasant” one but was necessary in order to alert the wider public to the issue.
Other members of Insulate Britain are also prominent members of XR, including Liam Norton, 36, an electrician from London who has represented the climate action group in the media.
“It’s a no-brainer,” he said. “Insulating Britain will reduce emissions, provide hundreds of thousands of jobs and stop our elderly dying in cold homes each winter.
“So stop messing about, Boris, and get on with the job. As soon as a statement is made that we can trust and is meaningful, we will get off the roads.”
Zoe Cohen, 51, another Insulate Britain activist, is also a member of XR and took part in their most recent protests in London last month.
Cohen, from Warrington, Cheshire, said: “Boris needs to stop making things worse — with all their road building, airport expansion, HS2 white elephant and new oil fields — and get on with the obvious stuff like insulating the 29 million homes that need to come off fossil fuels.”
Sean Martell, National Highways head of service delivery for the South East, said on Monday: “We work hard with police and other partners to limit the effects of protests on the strategic road network. We will do all we can to keep drivers up to date and on the move.”

https://www.thetimes.com/culture/tv-radi.title: Emilia Fox: my family, cousin Laurence and me
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/tv-radi.text:
The actress Emilia Fox has an imaginary friend. Her name is Nikki Alexander and she is a London-based clinical pathologist who’s a dab hand at gruesome autopsies. However, Fox thinks Nikki is a workaholic who should get a life. “She’s consumed by work and a bit isolated,” she says.
Fox-watchers will know that Nikki is also the character the 47-year-old actress has played these past 17 years in Silent Witness, the longest-running crime drama on British TV, but to Fox she is more real than that.
“I love that she is a friend and an ally to me in real life,” she says. “Seriously, she has been there for me in hard times. But if we were to go out for a drink together I would tell her to get some serious therapy and look after the other bits of her life.”
Terry Venables was the England football manager and the Spice Girls were releasing their debut single when Silent Witness started in 1996. Amanda Burton was the lead then. Fox donned the white germ suit in 2004. These days she knows her alter ego so well she can tell the Silence Witness writers when her character would or wouldn’t pour a glass of wine.
“We did a scene recently where Nikki was a bit reflective. They gave her a glass of wine. I didn’t think that was right. I can’t drink when I’m working any more so I said, ‘Can she do something else?’ When I reached my forties [Fox is 47], I was running between work and my daughter Rose and I had nothing else in my life.
“I was in therapy which has massively helped me. I decided getting physically fit would help my mental fitness so I started doing cardio, HIIT work-outs and Pilates. And so that fed into my character so we decided Nikki could go for a run instead.”
In real life Fox is doing somewhat better than her alter ego. Her soul-searching period is over. She is in love. “I am with someone and I am very happy and that’s a really lovely thing to be able to say,” she says with a smile.
Fox was married to Jared Harris (son of actor Richard), but they divorced in 2010 after five years. She subsequently had her daughter, Rose, with the film-maker and actor Jeremy Gilley and there have been rumoured romances with Charles Dance and Marco Pierre White.
For a long time she was a staunch advocate of single life, but in 2019 she met the talent agent Luc Chaudhary on the celebrity dating site Raya and there was talk of marriage. They split last year, with some tabloids suggesting she’d kicked him out until the couple released a joint statement on social media last October insisting that it was amicable.
“We ended on very good terms, but that was quite a long time ago. Then I had more time alone and I met someone new quite recently. I really appreciated every single second of my single life and I think I benefited from it. Hopefully, I’m now able to share life with someone with a better sense of self.”
Fox has been working in Italy for three months, but says her new beau is not Italian. Nor did she meet him via a dating app. “I’m a great believer in dating websites. I know so many people who have successfully found partners on them. All I can say is he is someone with understanding, kindness, thoughtfulness and a good moral compass.” She declines to say who he is, although a newspaper has since named him as Jonathan Stadlen, a 43-year-old television producer.
What makes a good man is a hot topic in the Fox family. We’re speaking days after her cousin Laurence tweeted stridently yet gnomically on the subject. “Bad times make hard men. Hard men make good times. Good times make soft men. Soft men make bad times. We are in bad times. We need principled MEN,” he tweeted.
Emilia has just returned from Rome. She loved the beautiful architecture. And, she says, they really know how to mix a negroni, but she has missed out on her cousin’s latest doings. “I’m not aware of the latest,” she says carefully.
In the spring Laurence was an unsuccessful candidate in London’s mayoral elections. He ran on an “anti-woke” ticket, fulminating against . . . well, you name it. He is anti-lockdown (he has called the Covid-19 pandemic “a scam” and “a mass delusion”), anti-vaccine, anti-mask wearing (he says masks are “woke burka-wearing” and making young people wear them is “child abuse”), anti-BBC children’s TV, anti-BLM and anti-Extinction Rebellion.
More recently, he has tweeted that we should “make” children head footballs. I don’t know if it was a coincidence, but the former Liverpool player Terry McDermott had announced he’d been diagnosed with dementia the day before.
Laurence and Emilia are close. In 2019 they appeared together on Channel 4’s Celebrity Gogglebox (afterwards she celebrated her “very funny wonderful cuz” on social media) and in February 2020 they did Top Gear (Laurence accused Emilia of being too nice a driver, letting people at junctions go first and too easily surrendering contested parking spaces. He then successfully navigated a series of bollards doing 110mph). She saluted that appearance with “luv u cuz”.
Yet today I have been told not to mention him. Why? “I don’t know what emails you’ve had, but Laurence is my cousin, he’s family and I love my family. I think he’d be the first to advocate that people can have different opinions on things.
“We’ve had very different life experiences and Laurence’s political life is nothing to do with my relationship with him. We’ve had some amazing times together and we’ve been very mutually supportive of our personal lives (Laurence was married to the actress Billie Piper married for nine years until 2016).
Is she worried about him? “Why should I be worried? What are the things you are worried about?” I mention that for an actor he doesn’t seem to be doing much acting. Last year his agent ditched him. Two weeks ago he was verbally assaulted outside Lord’s cricket ground. He has made a lot of enemies. “Laurence is well capable of standing on his own two feet,” she says crisply.
Yet loyalty can have a cost. Last year Emilia’s younger brother, the actor Freddie Fox, was spat at in the street as a result of his cousin’s views. Would Emilia, say, campaign on her cousin’s election “battle bus’’ if he stood for election again? “I wouldn’t go on anyone’s battle bus. And that’s got nothing to do with Laurence. That is just the last thing I’d ever do.”
I think we can safely say that she holds different views. When the lockdown halted production in 2020 the Silent Witness team gave all their PPE to the NHS. And Fox has followed the campaigning of Black Lives Matter and #MeToo with interest.
“BLM, #MeToo, issues around gender fluidity. So many lights are being shone on places which have remained in shadow for too long,” she says. “I think that has to be a positive thing about the times we are living in.”
Lockdown meant home-schooling Rose and only being able to see her mother and father, the actors Joanna David and Edward Fox, for three hours a week. Yet the Fox dynasty seemed to dominate our screens throughout the pandemic. As well as Top Gear with Laurence, Emilia appeared on Gogglebox and in All Round To Mrs Brown’s with her mother. David, who most recently played the Dowager Duchess of Yeovil in Downton Abbey, was momentarily the most controversial Fox family member when she exclaimed “F*** me!” on TV.
“Because of the roles she played in her career, people think she is an ingenue, the innocent one, but my mum can be outrageous. To be honest, I always felt like the boring one of the two of us.”
There was more family rivalry last year when her brother Freddie was cast as the notorious killer Jeremy Bamber in ITV’s true-crime drama White House Farm. The show was scheduled directly against Emilia in Silent Witness.
“That was awful. I don’t know why they did that. Anyway, I watched Fred and I thought he was terrific, but actually competition doesn’t come into it. I know how precarious acting can be. I know how hard it is not to have work. And there were times I felt, whenever I walked into a room, people were expecting a different Fox. I wanted to forge my own career, but it’s all very supportive now.”
That is beyond doubt. While she was in Rome, Emilia gave Freddie the keys to her London home. News for Laurence: he needed somewhere to isolate with a nasty case of coronavirus. “He wasn’t hospitalised, but he really wasn’t very well,” she says.
It seems it can be dangerous having young Freddie round at the best of times, especially if he brings his work home with him.“Freddie is quite methody in his approach to acting,” Emilia says. “ If he’s playing David Bowie, then he’ll sit there on a guitar being Bowie.
“When he came home one Christmas and told us he was going to play the killer Jeremy Bamber in White House Farm there was a sharp intake of breath [Bamber is serving a whole life tariff for killing his adoptive parents, sister and two six-year-old nephews in 1985 in order to secure an inheritance]. That certainly got everyone talking around the dinner table.”
She says her alter ego Nikki will go on investigating similarly terrible crimes for some time. Even after 17 years she loves her character and is growing with her. And there’s a bonus to this longevity. Silent Witness has given breaks to actors who have since become stars, such as Rory Kinnear, Idris Elba, Daniel Kaluuya, Benedict Cumberbatch and Jodie Comer.
Fox says she knows when a new star walks on set. She got the feeling with the new cast member Jason Wong, who plays the pushy young gun pathologist Adam Yuen. “I’ve worked with him before and I remember thinking, ‘He’s going to be a superstar.’ And he will be.”
Fox is content with her lot. Like Nikki Alexander, she used to be a workaholic and not take care of herself properly. Also like Nikki, the clues to the problem were often right in front of her. “I think we’ve all felt smaller and insignificant during the pandemic,” she says. “What I’ve learnt is: simplify things. You don’t need to chase what isn’t right in front of you.”Silent Witness returns tonight at 9pm on BBC1

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/wins.title: Winston Churchill Memorial Trust removes pictures over ‘unacceptable’ views on race
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/wins.text:
A charity set up to honour Sir Winston Churchill has removed all images of him from its website and rebranded itself after criticising his “unacceptable” views on race.
The Winston Churchill Memorial Trust has renamed itself the Churchill Fellowship and removed a 1,400-word article that desribed Churchill as a “much-loved leader”. A list of his achievements and a biography also appear to have been taken down.
In a blog titled Racism is Unacceptable, the charity acknowledged that there was controversy about comments made by Churchill. It praised him as a “leading social reformer” but said that it did not agree with his views on race.
“Today there is controversy about aspects of Sir Winston’s life. Many of his views on race are widely seen as unacceptable today, a view that we share,” a statement on the website said.
“At the same time, he is internationally admired for his wartime leadership in saving Britain and the world from Nazism. We acknowledge the many issues and complexities involved on all sides, but do not accept racism of any kind.”
A volunteer told The Sun that the name change was led by Julia Weston, the charity’s chief executive, and her board of trustees. In a recent email she is said to have told employees that “our previous name was confusing as it did not reflect what we are about”.
The trust was founded on February 1, 1965, two days after Churchill’s funeral. The Queen extended her patronage the same year.
For decades the charity has run a programme of overseas grants known as the Churchill Fellowships, which send 150 Britons a year to study abroad. It also funds up to ten undergraduate bursaries at Churchill College, Cambridge, and its board of trustees include Churchill’s grandson Jeremy Soames.
A spokesman for the charity said that it had retained Churchill’s surname and remained “proud of our connection to him and his contribution to saving the world from Nazism”. He added: “At the same time, some of his views on race are widely seen as unacceptable today.”
Historians have been at odds over the two-time prime minister’s legacy for decades, with many British scholars concluding that he was a great man despite his racist views, which were more common during his lifetime.
Born in 1874, he justified British imperialism as being for the good of the “primitive” and “subject races”. He was a believer in eugenics, supported the segregation of “feeble-minded” people and warned that the breeding of “unfit” people posed a “terrible danger to the race”.
Speaking about Native Americans and Aborigines in 1937, Churchill said: “I do not admit that a wrong has been done to those people by the fact that a stronger race, a higher-grade race, or, at any rate, a more worldly wise race . . . has come in and taken their place.”
Churchill’s critics have also pointed to his government’s failure to ship food to India during the 1943 Bengal famine, arguing that his actions were informed by his views on race and contributed to the death toll of up to three million people. Sir Max Hastings, the military historian, Times columnist and author of Winston’s War, said that Churchill’s behaviour during the Bengal famine was “a blot on his record” but should be weighed against his services to Britain and mankind.
In February a conference held at Churchill College to debate the “racial consequences” of his actions was told that he was the “perfect embodiment of white supremacy”.
Last June Extinction Rebellion activists painted the words “Churchill was a racist” on the college. Sir Nicholas Soames, the Conservative former MP and minister and another of Churchill’s grandsons, accused the activists of being “naive” and “idiotic”.
The Churchill statue in Parliament Square was also vandalised twice during Black Lives Matter protests last year.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.title: Chaos? This is nothing, warns Cambridge graduate who brought M25 to standstill
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.subtitle: Cathy Eastburn, 54, is one of Britain’s most prolific protesters and has been arrested at least 12 times in three years
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.text:
There are not many women who would protest topless outside parliament. Or superglue themselves to a commuter train. Or sit down on the M25.
However, Cathy Eastburn, 54, a Cambridge University philosophy graduate, is not most women.
She is revealed today as one of Britain’s most prolific and hardline climate change activists, having been arrested at least 12 times in under three years.
Eastburn specialises in what she describes as “high-stakes” or “high-risk” direct action. During the M25 protests by the Insulate Britain group, she was arrested four times in nine days, with police releasing her without charge each time to run amok again.
The soft-touch approach by law enforcement agencies caught even Eastburn by surprise. Her out-of-office response to emails states: “If you’re reading this, it is because I have been arrested and possibly put in prison on remand.”
However, she remains a free woman this weekend. “I haven’t even been interviewed by police,” she said.
The blockading of the UK’s busiest motorway on five days during rush-hour caused gridlock and risked fatal accidents. It cost workers millions in lost earnings. A woman who was being taken to hospital after a stroke is said to have been left paralysed because of the delays.
Eastburn, a sound therapist and professional musician, said she sympathised with those affected by the traffic jams but insisted that the protests had been “proportionate”.
“I’m not a disruptive person and I really feel for people who are caught up in the disruption,” she said. “Sitting in traffic for a few hours is awful but it’s incomparable to the kind of chaos that’s coming down the track — massive flooding and major food shortages.”
Although images of Eastburn repeatedly being carted off by police have been splashed across the media her identity was not commonly known until now.
Her four arrests on the M25 barely scratch the surface of her eco-activism.
A veteran Extinction Rebellion (XR) supporter, Eastburn has been involved in many high-profile stunts, including an attempt to confront Sir David Attenborough at his home, while he was shielding from the coronavirus, “for not telling the truth”.
Despite being briefly jailed twice, Eastburn, who is married with two daughters, aged 17 and 21, has usually managed to go free with a slap on the wrist.
She lives in a home that is worth almost £1 million near Clapham Common in south London and readily admits to being in a “privileged” position.
Eastburn performs as a singer and percussionist in an Indonesian-inspired gamelan ensemble and uses gongs and chanting as a form of stress- relief for clients.
“Not everyone is in a position to risk arrest or risk prison,” she said. “I think as a white middle-aged woman, it’s easier for me to go through the criminal justice system.”
Eastburn still feels she is making a “sacrifice”. “I don’t want to be spending my time in prison or spending my money on court costs. But it’s necessary. I’m doing this for my children and for children everywhere.”
She said that a UN report on global warming in 2018 prompted her to take part in non-violent direct action. The daughter of two school teachers from Cornwall, she likens her activism to that of the suffragettes and the US civil rights movement.
Eastburn was arrested and prosecuted for the first time in February 2019 after XR activists glued themselves to the doors of the InterContinental Hotel in London’s Park Lane as it hosted an oil conference.
About six weeks later she and two other protesters made headlines after bringing London’s Docklands Light Railway to a halt by gluing themselves to a train at Canary Wharf.
Eastburn was held on remand for just over a week at HMP Bronzefield near Ashford before being put on trial.
Jurors expressed “regret” after finding the trio guilty of obstructing the railway. They were each given a 12-month conditional discharge and ordered to pay costs.
In October 2019 Eastburn was arrested again, on suspicion of criminal damage, after a stunt involving fake blood being sprayed over the Treasury building in Whitehall.
Last September she was part of a group of women who removed their bras and locked themselves to railings outside the Houses of Parliament as part of wider XR protests across the capital.
“My younger daughter, who was 15 at the time, was mortified,” Eastburn admitted. She was also hauled away by police after blocking a nearby road. When she later appeared before Westminster magistrates, Eastburn illegally livestreamed the process of gluing herself to the wall of the dock. The action resulted in her being jailed for two weeks for contempt of court.
Her attempt to doorstep Attenborough, then 94, at his home in southwest London came after the naturalist and broadcaster warned people not to break the law for the green cause.
Eastburn argues that change can only come about through civil disobedience and that Attenborough, therefore, was “not telling the truth”.
She and five other XR activists approached the broadcaster’s house with gifts and an open letter in an attempt to “open a conversation” but Attenborough’s daughter told them that he was shielding.
Eastburn says she practises what she preaches. She is one of three vegans in her family and does not own a car.
Although she has made repeated trips to Indonesia in the past for her music career, she said she has given up flying. Speaking about her 12 arrests, Eastburn said: “I’m not proud of it. But I don’t feel what I’ve done is criminal. I feel like I’m preventing a far greater crime.”
